description:
Android's counterpart to `60`. Two source paths are stubbed: **seekable `content://` opening** and **provider staging**.

The asymmetry with iOS is real and worth respecting rather than abstracting away: a `content://` URI may or may not be seekable depending on the provider, and that is knowable only at runtime. When it is seekable, byte ranges stream and nothing is staged — the design commitment holds. When it is not, a staged copy is written under a reservation, which on Android means genuinely *reserving* space via `StorageManager.allocateBytes` rather than merely checking free space.

That reservation is the piece nothing off-the-shelf has, so it deserves a test that proves it actually reserves rather than just querying.

userStories.title: A seekable content:// source streams without staging
userStories.description: Detect seekability at runtime and take the no-copy path whenever it is available.
acceptanceCriteria: Seekability is determined at runtime, not assumed from the URI scheme.
A seekable source streams byte ranges with no staged copy — asserted by checking that no staging file is created.
A test covers both a seekable and a non-seekable provider.
userStories.notes: SourceResolver probes ParcelFileDescriptor.seekTo at runtime and streams seekable descriptors through FileChannel; Swift build/tests green (42 passed), TypeScript typecheck green; Android Gradle unavailable locally.

userStories.title: Non-seekable providers stage under a real StorageManager reservation
userStories.description: `allocateBytes` genuinely reserves; a free-space check does not. The difference is the whole point.
acceptanceCriteria: Staging calls `StorageManager.allocateBytes` rather than reading free space.
A denied allocation fails the job with a typed error instead of proceeding and failing later.
The staged copy is removed on completion, cancel and failure.
A test asserts the allocation call is actually made, not merely that staging succeeded.
